quotes.quote: Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block printing technique that involves series of direct and resist printing and dyeing to create unique effects.
Ajrakh is a unique combination of hand block printing and resist dyeing.

Ajrakh is a double-sided, block-printed textile worn as caste dress by cattle herders in the desert regions of Kachchh and Thar in north-west India and Sindh in Pakistan, where it is made by Khatri artisans.
The Ajrakh traditions are maintained in three villages of Kutch district namely Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda.
The production of Ajrakh is now restricted to only three centers, namely Dhamadka, Khavda and Ajrakhpur.
Traditionally four colours were used i.e., blue, black, red and white.
For a piece to be called ajrakh, it needs to have all the four colours, blue, red, black and white.
is traditionally blue with red, black, and white patterns of classic Islamic style
it has also become the signature cloth of the Khatri communities at Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur in Kachchh and is their most successful product.
The process and designs of Ajrakh printing are common to Sindh (now in Pakistan), Kutch and Barmer district of Rajasthan.
The origin of ajrakh can be traced to Sind, Pakistan.
The origin of Ajrakh can be traced to Sind, Pakistan.
Ajrakh printing originally came from Sindh and got concentrated where extra soft water was available.
The artisans who made these textiles belonged to the Khatri community (both Hindus /Muslims)
Most of the artisans of Kutch and Barmer believe that their ancestors were from Sindh, and even now many of their relatives live in the Sindh region.
Originally from Sindh, the Khatris practice crafts like block print, batik print, tie and dye, and rogan painting.
The erstwhile ruler of Kutch Rao Bharmalji - I (1586-1631), invited the cloth-printing Khatri artisans from Sindh and gave them permission to settle and earn their livelihoods anywhere in Kutch.
They were given land by the state as well spared any taxation on their produce.

Rao Barmalji I, the King of Kachchh, was a patron of craft. He invited artisans from across Sindh to come and settle in his kingdom. We were given land and accommodations. Even the taxes were cancelled for us.
The respondent mentioned that Raja Bharmalji I of Bhuj had brought the artisans from Sindh, Pakistan to this part of Gujarat.
Rao Bharmalji, a ruler of sixteenth-century Kutch and patron of the arts, brought the Khatris to his kingdom.

many of the Khatri ajrakh printers in Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur are closely related, descended from a common forefather, Jindha Jiva, who founded Dhamadka during the reign of Rao Bharmal I of Kachchh (r. 1586-1631) - they belong to the same (Dhadha) clan.

According to popular legend, this textile tradition was started in the family of late Mohammad Siddiki when in the year 1586, Raja Bharmal I, invited his forefathers, to migrate from Sind and settle in Dhamadka, Kachchh.
The Ajrakh activities prevailed at Dhamadka since the past 450 years, as it was having a potential water source from one of the water stream of the Indus river.
A trefoil pattern is carved into his shawl. Block printers will identify the trefoil motif as kakkar, a cloud pattern common to the traditional Ajrakh patterns made in Sindh and Kachchh.
The celebrated statue of the King Priest discovered at Moenjodaro has a trefoil motif on the draped shawl. The ajrak craftsmen claim that the pattern is kakar, a cloud pattern.
The bust of the Priest King of Mohenjo Daro depicts him wrapped in a shawl with trefoil motifs, similar to the kakar or cloud motif seen in ajrakh prints.
In 1930, hundreds of Indian cotton fragments from the 11th-14th century AD were discovered in Al Fustat, the harbor of Old Cairo.
They remain the earliest example of block printed cloth.
In 1930, hundreds of cotton fragments were retrieved from Al Fustat - harbor of Old Cairo - dating from the 11th to the 14th century AD. These fragments are the earliest known printed textiles.
The simple patterns printed with small sized blocks, resist dyed in indigo and madder, bear a striking similarity to ajrak.
The Al Fustat textiles were printed using small blocks, natural colors, and simple patterns. Similar designs are still being printed in modern-day Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur.

So people from our village came together and bought land 40 kms away from Dhamadka. One member was identified from ten main families who would together take key decisions. We called the new village Ajrakhpur.

1 Saaj no Marhalo: First, the fabric is washed in plain water and beaten to remove all the impurities from the fabric.

Traditionally, the procedure for this was soaking of fabric in soda ash, castor oil and then, further soaking it in camel dung solution to make the fabric soft, which acted as a bleaching agent (alkaline).
In Kachchh, pre-treatment of the cotton involves a minimum of three soakings in Neerani solution. This is a thoroughly emulsified mixture of castor oil, soda ash and camel dung.
The cloth is kneaded in this Neerani mixture wrung out, then bundled-up and wrapped in Hessain cloth, secured by a heavy stone or rock, and left to steep overnight.
To remove impurities and prepare for printing, cloth is soaked in a solution of castor oil, camel dung, and soda ash. This mixture is known as saaji. Cloth is left overnight to soak.
The entire procedure is repeated eight to ten times until a suitable level of saponification is achieved
which leaves the cloth bright white and soft to touch.
Saaj and the drying stage are repeated (7-9 times) until the cloth foams when rubbed. It is then washed in plain water.
This process is repeated several times until the cloth foams when rubbed.
2 Kasanu/Harda treatment: The next stage consisted of treating the fabric with harda (myrobalan).
This is done by soaking the fabric in harda solution, pounding the fabric with the feet, removing from the solution, drying and beating the dried fabric to dust off extra harda powder.
these dried plums contain high levels of Tannic acid.
The tannin in the Myroballan penetrates the cotton fibres and is essential pre-mordant which aids the adhesion of the subsequent printed mordants onto the cloth.
3 Rekh (outline) printing: Gum arabic and lime are mixed for kiryana (printing of the white outlines).
Preparation of Outline of design (Khariyanu/ Kiriyana):- Outlines of the design, where white is required, are printed with a carved wooden block and a resist paste containing lime and tree gum.
The morning time is usually preferred for this stage of printing.
If the fabric had to be printed double sided, then they are printed on the reverse side with rekh blocks.

When double sided Ajrakh is printed it is essential that the same outline design be printed on the reverse of the cloth. A printer must be very accurate to ensure designs match precisely on both the sides and the fabric should be partly wet to ensure proper registration.
This is helped by small registration marks on the corners of the symmetrically patterned blocks.
Care must be taken not to mix this Pa with the areas printed in lime Khariyanu otherwise the lime will discharge the alum and thus prevent colour developing during subsequent red dyeing.
this must not spread onto areas where red is required or the lime will discharge the subsequent applications of alum.
a paste made of lime (calcium hydroxide) and gum from the babul or acacia tree (Acacia nilotica indica)
The latter resist is used for contemporary ajrakh
Gum and lime are the most preferred resit materials today by the Ajrakh block printers.
While Ajrakh and most related cloths are resist printed with a gum arabic and lime substance

4 Drying of rekh printed fabric: After printing the fabric with rekh (outlines), the fabric is dried in sun and if the fa bric is to be printed both the sides, the fabric is reversed to dry on the other side.
5 Kat (black) printing: Gum, ferrous sulphate, fuller's earth and water are used to make the black outlines.
These ingredients were traditionally used but today, the process of kat printing is carried out using scrap iron, kachuka no loat (tamarind seeds powder) and gud (jaggery) to make paste.
The kut is a smooth finer paste made from jaggery, or molasses, in which scrap iron such as horse-hoes and besan (gram flour) have been fermented for ten to fifteen days.
Scrap iron, jaggery and tamarind is soaked in water for two weeks and then cooked over flame to create the black dye for Ajrakh.
This mixture is left to ferment which takes about one week in the hot season and two weeks during the cold season; a yellowish scum on the surface of the mixture indicates that it is ready for use.
When printed onto the harde treated cloth kut develops a deep fast chocolate-black colour as the iron particles in the kut paste oxidise with the tannic acid.
These lines oxidise when exposed to air and the harda and develop a black colour.
6 Phulli/Kan printing: Resisting of small star like areas, where Kachuka no lot (tamarind seeds powder), is mixed in alum and then boiled for 1 hr to produce a thick printing paste.
To this, some amount of fugitive dye, k esari rang, is added to separate this paste from the other printed resist pastes.
Traditionally, geru is used instead of fugitive dye. The fabric is now stamped with this paste.
The mordant, alum required for producing red is now applied to the cloth. Alum is suspended in a sticky paste of boiled powder from roasted and ground tamarind seeds (locally known as kachika).

This smooth paste called Pa, is printed with blocks which have been carved so that the printing portion of the raised face is patterned only, with the areas of the design called mavi, where red is required.

7 Gach/ Khor printing: The first part of this stage is called khor printing, where the resist is prepared with a paste of alum, gum arabic, millet flour and red clay and is stamped on the fabric with the help of filler block ( gadh).
The later step of this stage includes the stamping of resist paste made of lime and gum arabic.
traditionally powder of dried Bakri ni lindi (goat excreta) is sprinkled, which prevent the smudging of design.
The clay and millet flour in the paste act as a resist, preventing indigo from staining the cloth beneath, whilst the alum content acts a mordant for subsequent application of red dye.
8 Indigo dyeing I: Traditionally, natural indigo is used and the naand ('V' shaped container), that was dug in ground is used for dyeing.
The indigo along with kuwadia na beej (casatoria seeds) is added in naand containing water and is left for months for the growth of bacteria. Then, the fabric is dyed in it for 10-15 min.
Today, the synthetic indigo is put along with sodium hydrosuphite and caustic soda in the maat (clay container) containing water. The maat is left to mature for 3-4 days
In order to establish an indigo vat, natural indigo, sagikhar (a salt), lime, casiatora (seed from kuwada plant) and water are mixed in a clay vessel, plastic barrel or concrete vat.
The dye bath is left to ferment for about one month; sometimes jaggery is added to this to aid fermentation.
At first bright green, the cloth rapidly becomes blue as oxygen meets the dye particles on the fibres.
The dyed cloth emerges a bright green that slowly turns blue once the dye oxidises.
If a design required the darkest shades of the blue then the cloth may be subjected to a total of three or four immersions into the vat to build up rich blue.
if two shades of the blue are required in the design then cloth is reprinted between the immersions into the Indigo vat, to preserve areas of the lighter blue achieved from the first dip.

9 Vichharnu: The indigo dyed fabric is washed in running water and laid flat to dry in sun. Fabric is not vigorously rubbed and the khor resist is not removed and hence the resultant fabric remains stiff.

10 Rang: For this step, the cloth is boiled with dhaori na phool (galls of tamarisk) and majith (madder) with sufficient amount of water in the charu of rangchul (metal container fixed on a stand) for 2-3 hrs.
The fabric is then washed in running water and dried in sun.
Alizarin crystals or the crushed and steeped roots of majeeta or Indian Madder are gently heated in a large copper pot.
The fire beneath is kept low and the lengths of cloth continuously
Dyeing the purest reds continues for up to four hours.
Steps 7 to 10 are repeated once again to get brighter and more brilliant shades of red and blue.

11. Gach (alum printing - see 7) is repeated. The cloth is left for several days after this. This stage is known as minakari (from Persian, refers to enamelling but used in Kachchh to mean 'double work')
Indian Madder roots, Rubia Cordifolia, locally known as majeeta, have been traditionally used in the creation of Ajrakh
This dye extracted from these long thin roots links to the alum mordant on the cotton fibres and develops red area of a design, where Pa, Gach pastes have been printed.
Alizarin was one of the first chemical dyes for red, invented in 1868 by German chemists Graaebe and Liebermann.
Derived from coal tar this crystalline red dye rapidly superseded madder, its natural counterpart.
Despite its chemical synthesis, alizarin dye also requires mordants such as alum to attach its colour to the cloth fibres.
uses synthetic forms of madder (alizarin) and indigo ('German indigo')
chemically identical to the natural dyestuffs but far cheaper, they are easy to use, reliable and available in large quantities.

The color compounds contained within natural madder roots are much more complex than those of synthetic alizarin. As a result dyeing with majeeta often leaves a pinkish tinge to the white areas of a design.
The dyed cloth would be soaked in a solution of camel dung, then spread on the sandy banks of a river in the sun and regularly sprinkled with water to keep it moist throughout the day.
This would be repeated over at least three days, by the end of which the sun, moisture and various compound in the dung would have acted as a bleaching agent on the white areas of a design.
The process of ajrakh printing is laborious and includes 14 stages. Each stage requires different tools and ingredients.
Appendix A: Fourteen Stages of Ajrakh
In total, 15-16 different stages are involved in the process of dyeing and printing, which take approximately 15-21 days.
It is a water-intensive, 16-stage process that takes time and is much in demand among Indian and international buyers.
The cloth is made in a sixteen step process of washing, dyeing, printing, and drying, with one step being performed in one day and the fabric being put to rest for the day.

The artisans use only wooden blocks in preparing Ajrakh print as wood absorbs the color better and more uniformly. The blocks used in the first stage of printing are made of shisham and the blocks used in the third and fourth stages are made of teak.
The blocks are soaked in mustard oil when not in use so that they do not expand in the rainy season.
The pors are carved from the Acacia Arabica trees, indigenous to the Sindh region.
The blocks are carved in pairs that can register an exact inverted image on the other side.
The printing blocks are often carved in pairs, thus registering an exact inverted image on the other side of the cloth.
The equipments, like rangchul (tank for dyeing) were made using bricks and cow dung. Charu (pot in the rangchul) was made traditionally out of aluminium.

patterns of classic Islamic style, based on mizan (balance or order) and geometry.
Traditional Ajrakh textiles have a fixed layout. They feature a large central body, with a repeated motif on a tight grid, border and end panels.
Both ends of the cloth are decorated while three sides have embellished borders, whose designs are fixed. Only the motif in the centre of the cloth may be changed.
today include between twenty-five and thirty designs, according to Abduljabbar M. Khatri of Dhamadka, one of the leading producers of ajrakh in Kachchh.

An Ajrakh, a rectangular cloth, made in two parts stitched together, has a fixed set of multiple borders on its long and short sides, and a field with one of about sixteen patterns.
We have a portfolio of 16 traditional ajrakh designs
Each pattern is created with impressions of three blocks, an outline called rekh, and two filling patterns called datlo-one for each color; all patterns must register.

Traditional blocks, called char pa ek (four parts to one), in which motifs are created by registering four impressions, have been abandoned for a style called sal type (flush joining), in which the entire motif is on one block.
Printing with these blocks is faster, though less perfect-suited for cheap, scaled-up production.

This magnificent textile has a peculiar characteristic of being stitched from centre. The reason for this was, earlier the fabrics were woven in to small width and hence to produce a normal width of fabric, small pieces of fabric were stitched together.
The fabric so produced of ajrakh was called Bi-poti ajrakh.
Earlier, when the fabric used was woven on the pit looms, the required width of fabric was acquired by joining two narrow width lengths with use of a decorative joining stitch.
Ajrakh is of two types - ek-puri, which is printed only on one side and bi-puri, which is printed on both sides.
The most highly prized Ajrakh textiles were bipuri, i.e. the ones printed identically on both sides.
the most acclaimed is a double-faced textile, printed on both sides of the fabric, dyed using madder and indigo, and known as minakari.
tested by holding the finished cloth up to the sun, thus revealing any mistakes, requires the utmost skill on the part of the artisan.
Legends say this was made because the Maldhari men needed to get dressed before the sun rose in order to herd their livestock.
would leave their homes even before sun rise and there was no electricity in those times so they couldn"t differentiate the right side from the wrong side in darkness.
In the most traditional version, the fabric is painstakingly printed on both sides with exact registration, dyed, washed, and then printed on both sides and dyed again.
This creates deeper shades of indigo and madder, extends the life of the cloth, and enables it to be used as a turban or shoulder cloth in which no reverse side shows.

Khatris knew their clients intimately, usually through hereditary relationships, passed down through generations.
They bartered their dyed fabrics directly to their users for milk, animals, and grain.
They used the barter system and exchanged cloth for produce from farmers, while cattle herders gave them milk or ghee.
Muslim Maldhari men, or cattle herders, wore Ajrakh as a poth (lungi, or lower wrap), turban, and shoulder cloth
The traditional purchasers of Ajrakh were Muslim nomadic animal-keepers, a group that still survives. In Kutch (Gujarat) this community is referred to as Maldharis.
Ajrakh is the traditional attire of the Muslim Maldharis, the pastoral communities from the region. An Ajrakh turban was a gift for the Maldhari groom at the time of marriage.
These days the Khatri artisans of Kutch have almost stopped producing Ajrakh prints for their traditional Maldhari customers

Maldharis still wear Ajrakh cloth today. However, due to change in practices, the traditional hand block printed, natural dyed Ajrakh is no longer affordable for them. They purchase either the screen-printed substitutes or the Ajrakh block prints from Sindh.
